## **Homework 3, Part 3**
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><i>The spy saw the agent with the binoculars on the roof</i>.</h3>
</div>
<br><br>
- draw syntax trees for the original sentence, NOT the interpretations<br><br>
- so the main idea here is to capture different **modification** relation on **the same sentence**, which reflects **structural difference** on the tree
  
---
## **Syntax Rules Across Languages**
<br>
.pull-left[
speakers of different languages will have different syntax rules
- because they have different mental grammars<br><br>

consider these phrases from **different languages**:<br><br>
- for each phrase, I've given a simplified version of a phrase structure rule for English<br><br>
- how would you modify that rule to account for each phrase?<br><br>
- what would you have to change?<br><br>
- assume that these languages place each adjective in an AdjP and each noun in an NP, as English does
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
English Rule: <b>NP → D AdjP N</b>
</div>

***Portuguese***

  <tr>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">a</td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">casa</td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">amarela</td>
  </tr>
    <tr>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;"></td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">the</td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">house</td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">yellow</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;"></td>
    <td colspan="3" style="text-align:left; padding-bottom:20px;">
    '<i>the yellow house</i>'</td>
  </tr>
</table>
<div style="text-align:center">
English Rule: <b>PP → P NP</b>
</div>

***Japanese***
<table style="width:100%; table-layout:auto; border-collapse:collapse;">
  <tr>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">gakkō</td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">de</td>
  </tr>
    <tr>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;"></td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">school</td>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;">at</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="white-space:nowrap;"></td>

    '<i>at school</i>'</td>
  </tr>

***Quechua***

## **Syntactic Transformations**
<br>
- once we understand how to draw a syntax tree for a simple sentence, we can use it as a basis for
more complex ideas, such as **syntactic transformations**<br><br>
- for example, we can say the following sentence because it follows English rules: TP → NP T VP

<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0302/trans1.png" width="25%">
<br><i>'You can play piano.'</i>.
</div>
<br>

- but what if we made it a question: ***Can you play piano?***
  
---
## **Syntactic Transformations**
<br>
- to make questions, we need to apply **transformations**: move constituents about in the tree<br><br>
- move <u><i>can</i></u> **up into** another level above TP: now we have a **yes-no question**!
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0302/trans1.png" width="23%"><span style="color:#CC0033"><b>→</b></span><img src="../pic/0302/trans2.png" width="29%">
</div>


---
## **Syntactic Transformations**
<br>
.pull-left[
what if we wanted to make a wh- question<br><br>
- ***What can you play?***
]
.pull-right[
- what does <u><i>what</i></u> represent?<br><br>
- **replace **piano with <u><i>what</i></u> and **move** it one level above <u><i>can</i></u>
]
<br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0302/trans2.png" width="28%"><span style="color:#CC0033"><b>→</b></span><img src="../pic/0302/trans3.png" width="26%">
</div>

## **How well do you know each of these topics?**
<br>
.pull-left[
**basic concepts in Linguistics**
- mental grammar/linguistic competence
- descriptivism vs. prescriptivism
- Grammatical vs. ungrammatical language
- standard vs. non-standard language <br><br>

**Syntax**
- parts of speech: definitions of nouns, verbs, etc.
- parts of speech: morphological and syntactic distribution of nouns, verbs, etc.
- constituents
- phrase structure rules (PSRs)
- types of phrases: NP, AdjP, AdvP, PP, VP, TP
- complex sentences: main and dependent clauses, complementisers, CP
- sentences and tree structure
]
.pull-right[
**Morphology**
- morphemes
- roots vs. affixes
- roots vs. stems
- types of affixes
- free vs. bound morphemes
- derivational vs. inflectional morphemes
- allomorphs
- monomorphemic and polymorphemic words
- simple and compound words
- morphological processes
  - affixation
  - compounding
  - reduplication
  - alternation
  - suppletion
  - zero-derivation
- order of affixation
]


---
## **How well can you apply<br> these analytical tools in practice?**
<br>
.pull-left[
- break down words **into morphemes** and identify the **type** of each morpheme<br><br>
- identify specific **morphological processes**<br><br>
- analyze the morphological structure of an **unfamiliar language**<br><br>
- draw a **morphological tree** to illustrate a word’s structure and **order of affixation**<br><br>
- identify a word’s **part of speech**<br><br>
- use morphological and syntactic **distribution** to determine a word’s part of speech
]
.pull-right[
- use **constituency tests** to determine if a sequence of words is a constituent<br><br>
- identify different **types of phrase**: NP, PP, AdjP, AdvP, VP, TP<br><br>
- identify the **head** of a phrase<br><br>
- use **phrase structure rules** to combine words into phrases<br><br>
- draw **syntax trees** to illustrate a sentence’s internal structure<br><br>
]
